title: Unsupervised Deep Equilibrium Model Learning for Large-Scale Channel Estimation with Performance Guarantees
venue: arXiv preprint (presented in part at IEEE GLOBECOM 2024)

citations.claim: Tian and Lian proposed an unsupervised DEQ learning framework (GUDL) for large-scale channel estimation that does not require ground-truth labels, using Generalized Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate (GSURE) as the loss function.
Deep unrolling suffers from numerical instability in training and high storage costs, making it difficult to increase the number of unrolled iterations sufficiently, which limits performance.

DEQ directly learns the fixed point of a nonlinear mapping with constant memory, and backpropagation can be conducted at the fixed point through implicit differentiation, requiring only constant memory.

Tian and Lian proved that DEQ with a contraction mapping inherently enforces a compressible (sparse) output structure, and that this property combined with GSURE-based PMSE minimization provides theoretical performance guarantees approaching oracle-level supervised accuracy.
The DEQ model structure was derived from a proximal gradient descent algorithm, where the proximal operator is replaced by a neural network to learn the optimal denoising function directly from data.

Convergence of DEQ is guaranteed by designing the mapping function as a contraction mapping with Lipschitz constant L in (0,1), ensuring linear convergence to a unique fixed point for any initialization.

An inexact gradient estimate can be used for DEQ backpropagation, where the matrix inversion in the Jacobian vanishes, and this approximation is proven to be a descent direction of the loss under mild conditions.
Supervised channel learning methods based on deep unrolling and DEQ allow convergence analysis by establishing a correspondence with underlying iterative algorithms.

do_not_claim: GUDL was applied to baseline correction, chromatography, or spectroscopy
GUDL uses algorithm unrolling (it uses DEQ as an alternative to unrolling)
GUDL works with 1D signals like chromatograms (it addresses large-scale MIMO channel estimation)
GUDL demonstrates that unsupervised learning always matches supervised performance (it provides theoretical bounds on the gap)
